title: Gaps and islands
summary_md: Find unbroken runs (islands) and the holes between them: streaks, longest consecutive days, missing dates and ids, runs of the same status. One trick covers almost all of it: value minus ROW_NUMBER is constant inside a run.

sections.heading: Consecutive days: the row-number trick
sections.body_md:
**Cue:** "consecutive days", "streak", "in a row", "unbroken run", "N days straight".

**Shape (always the same 4 steps):**
- Reduce to one row per (entity, day) with `SELECT DISTINCT`. Duplicates break the trick.
- `ROW_NUMBER()` per entity ordered by day -> `rn`.
- `day - rn` days = a constant per unbroken run. Call it the island key `grp`.
- `GROUP BY entity, grp` -> `MIN(day)`, `MAX(day)`, `COUNT(*)` = start, end, length.

**Why it works:** inside a run both `day` and `rn` rise by 1 per row, so their difference stays fixed. A missing day makes `day` jump by 2 while `rn` rises by 1, so the key changes.

syntax.mysql: DATE_SUB(day_col, INTERVAL ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY entity ORDER BY day_col) DAY)
syntax.tsql: DATEADD(day, -ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY entity ORDER BY day_col), day_col)

args.name: day_col
args.meaning: A DATE column, already de-duplicated to one row per entity per day.

args.name: PARTITION BY entity
args.meaning: Restart the numbering for each user/device/account so streaks never span two entities.

args.name: ORDER BY day_col
args.meaning: Numbering follows calendar order; this is what makes day minus rn constant inside a run.

args.name: INTERVAL ... DAY / day, -n
args.meaning: Subtract rn calendar days. T-SQL negates the number because DATEADD adds.

examples.title: Step 1-2: one row per user-day, then number them
examples.explain_md: `DISTINCT` collapses user 2's two events at the same second (and any same-day repeats) into one row. User 3 has days 1, 2, 3 and 5 May, so `rn` runs 1-4.
examples.mysql:
WITH days AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT user_id, DATE(event_ts) AS active_day
  FROM events
)
SELECT user_id, active_day,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY active_day) AS rn
FROM days
ORDER BY user_id, active_day;
examples.tsql:
WITH days AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT user_id, CAST(event_ts AS DATE) AS active_day
  FROM events
)
SELECT user_id, active_day,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY active_day) AS rn
FROM days
ORDER BY user_id, active_day;

examples.title: Step 3: subtract rn days to get the island key
examples.explain_md: User 3: May 1-3 all map to the same `grp` (2024-04-30); May 5 maps to 2024-05-01. Different key = different island. The key is not a meaningful date, only a label.
examples.mysql:
WITH days AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT user_id, DATE(event_ts) AS active_day FROM events
), numbered AS (
  SELECT user_id, active_day,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY active_day) AS rn
  FROM days
)
SELECT user_id, active_day, rn,
       DATE_SUB(active_day, INTERVAL rn DAY) AS grp
FROM numbered
ORDER BY user_id, active_day;
examples.tsql:
WITH days AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT user_id, CAST(event_ts AS DATE) AS active_day FROM events
), numbered AS (
  SELECT user_id, active_day,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY active_day) AS rn
  FROM days
)
SELECT user_id, active_day, rn,
       DATEADD(day, -rn, active_day) AS grp
FROM numbered
ORDER BY user_id, active_day;

examples.title: Step 4: collapse each island
examples.explain_md: One row per run. User 3 has a 3-day island and a 1-day island; users 1 and 2 have a single island each.
examples.mysql:
WITH days AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT user_id, DATE(event_ts) AS active_day FROM events
), numbered AS (
  SELECT user_id, active_day,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY active_day) AS rn
  FROM days
), keyed AS (
  SELECT user_id, active_day, DATE_SUB(active_day, INTERVAL rn DAY) AS grp
  FROM numbered
)
SELECT user_id, MIN(active_day) AS streak_start, MAX(active_day) AS streak_end,
       COUNT(*) AS streak_days
FROM keyed
GROUP BY user_id, grp
ORDER BY user_id, streak_start;
examples.tsql:
WITH days AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT user_id, CAST(event_ts AS DATE) AS active_day FROM events
), numbered AS (
  SELECT user_id, active_day,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY active_day) AS rn
  FROM days
), keyed AS (
  SELECT user_id, active_day, DATEADD(day, -rn, active_day) AS grp
  FROM numbered
)
SELECT user_id, MIN(active_day) AS streak_start, MAX(active_day) AS streak_end,
       COUNT(*) AS streak_days
FROM keyed
GROUP BY user_id, grp
ORDER BY user_id, streak_start;

examples.title: Trap: skipping the dedupe step
examples.explain_md: User 1 logged in twice on 06-02. Without `DISTINCT`, `rn` keeps counting the duplicate, so `day - rn` shifts: the 06-01..06-03 run splits (06-03 gets 2024-05-30, 06-01 gets 2024-05-31) and 06-05 collides with 06-01 (both 2024-05-31), merging unrelated days. Always dedupe to one row per entity-day first.

tables.name: logins
tables.description_md: One row per login event. User 1 logged in twice on 2024-06-02 (duplicate day). User 4's run crosses a month end.

examples.mysql:
WITH numbered AS (
  SELECT user_id, login_date,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY login_date) AS rn
  FROM logins
  WHERE user_id = 1
)
SELECT user_id, login_date, rn, DATE_SUB(login_date, INTERVAL rn DAY) AS grp
FROM numbered
ORDER BY login_date, rn;
examples.tsql:
WITH numbered AS (
  SELECT user_id, login_date,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY login_date) AS rn
  FROM logins
  WHERE user_id = 1
)
SELECT user_id, login_date, rn, DATEADD(day, -rn, login_date) AS grp
FROM numbered
ORDER BY login_date, rn;

pitfalls_md: No dedupe -> duplicate days shift `rn` and fragment the streak.
If the grain is a timestamp, cast to DATE first (`DATE(ts)` / `CAST(ts AS DATE)`), then dedupe.
Works for gapless integer sequences too (`id - rn`), and across month/year ends because it is real date arithmetic.

sections.heading: Streak length, longest streak, current streak
sections.body_md:
**Cue:** "longest streak", "max consecutive days", "users with N+ days in a row", "current streak".

**Shape:** build the `islands` CTE once (dedupe -> rn -> key -> aggregate), then answer any streak question by filtering or ranking the islands.
- Longest per user: `ROW_NUMBER() ... ORDER BY streak_days DESC` then `rk = 1`, or `MAX(streak_days)` if only the number is needed.
- Streak of at least N: `WHERE streak_days >= N`.
- Current streak: cut activity at the as-of date, keep the island whose end is the as-of day or the day before.

examples.title: Every streak per user
examples.explain_md: The `islands` CTE is reused in the next examples. User 4 stays one 3-day island across the May/June boundary.

tables.name: logins
tables.description_md: One row per login event. User 1 logged in twice on 2024-06-02 (duplicate day). User 4's run crosses a month end.

examples.title: Longest streak per user (with tie-break)
examples.explain_md: `ROW_NUMBER` keeps exactly one island per user. User 1 has a 3-day (06-01..03) and 2-day islands; user 2 has a 1-day and a 4-day. The tie-break (`streak_start DESC` = most recent) must be stated; use `RANK` instead if the question wants all tied islands.

tables.name: logins
tables.description_md: One row per login event. User 1 logged in twice on 2024-06-02 (duplicate day). User 4's run crosses a month end.

examples.mysql:
WITH days AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT user_id, login_date FROM logins
), numbered AS (
  SELECT user_id, login_date,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY login_date) AS rn
  FROM days
), islands AS (
  SELECT user_id, MIN(login_date) AS streak_start, MAX(login_date) AS streak_end,
         COUNT(*) AS streak_days
  FROM (SELECT user_id, login_date, DATE_SUB(login_date, INTERVAL rn DAY) AS grp FROM numbered) k
  GROUP BY user_id, grp
)
, ranked AS (
  SELECT islands.*,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY streak_days DESC, streak_start DESC) AS rk
  FROM islands
)
SELECT user_id, streak_start, streak_end, streak_days
FROM ranked
WHERE rk = 1
ORDER BY user_id;
examples.tsql:
WITH days AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT user_id, login_date FROM logins
), numbered AS (
  SELECT user_id, login_date,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY login_date) AS rn
  FROM days
), islands AS (
  SELECT user_id, MIN(login_date) AS streak_start, MAX(login_date) AS streak_end,
         COUNT(*) AS streak_days
  FROM (SELECT user_id, login_date, DATEADD(day, -rn, login_date) AS grp FROM numbered) k
  GROUP BY user_id, grp
)
, ranked AS (
  SELECT islands.*,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY streak_days DESC, streak_start DESC) AS rk
  FROM islands
)
SELECT user_id, streak_start, streak_end, streak_days
FROM ranked
WHERE rk = 1
ORDER BY user_id;

examples.title: Users who ever had a streak of at least 3 days
examples.explain_md: Filter on the island length, then `DISTINCT` the user (a user can have several qualifying islands). If only the best length is needed, `MAX(streak_days)` per user is enough.

tables.description_md: One row per login event. User 1 logged in twice on 2024-06-02 (duplicate day). User 4's run crosses a month end.

examples.title: Current streak as of a date
examples.explain_md: Ignore activity after the as-of date, then keep only islands that end on the as-of day or the day before (a streak is still alive if today is empty but yesterday is not). User 1's 06-10 login is after the as-of date; user 4's streak ended 06-01 so it is dead.

tables.name: logins
tables.description_md: One row per login event. User 1 logged in twice on 2024-06-02 (duplicate day). User 4's run crosses a month end.

examples.mysql:
WITH days AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT user_id, login_date FROM logins
  WHERE login_date <= CAST('2024-06-06' AS DATE)
), numbered AS (
  SELECT user_id, login_date,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY login_date) AS rn
  FROM days
), islands AS (
  SELECT user_id, MIN(login_date) AS streak_start, MAX(login_date) AS streak_end,
         COUNT(*) AS streak_days
  FROM (SELECT user_id, login_date, DATE_SUB(login_date, INTERVAL rn DAY) AS grp FROM numbered) k
  GROUP BY user_id, grp
)
SELECT user_id, streak_days AS current_streak
FROM islands
WHERE streak_end >= DATE_SUB(CAST('2024-06-06' AS DATE), INTERVAL 1 DAY)
ORDER BY user_id;
examples.tsql:
WITH days AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT user_id, login_date FROM logins
  WHERE login_date <= CAST('2024-06-06' AS DATE)
), numbered AS (
  SELECT user_id, login_date,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY login_date) AS rn
  FROM days
), islands AS (
  SELECT user_id, MIN(login_date) AS streak_start, MAX(login_date) AS streak_end,
         COUNT(*) AS streak_days
  FROM (SELECT user_id, login_date, DATEADD(day, -rn, login_date) AS grp FROM numbered) k
  GROUP BY user_id, grp
)
SELECT user_id, streak_days AS current_streak
FROM islands
WHERE streak_end >= DATEADD(day, -1, CAST('2024-06-06' AS DATE))
ORDER BY user_id;

pitfalls_md: State the tie-break for longest streak (earliest, latest, or all tied via `RANK`).
Current streak: decide whether yesterday-only counts as alive, and filter out future-dated rows.
Streaks of weekdays only or business days need a calendar table; plain date arithmetic counts weekends as gaps.

sections.heading: Finding gaps
sections.body_md:
**Cue:** "find missing dates", "periods with no activity", "inactive for more than N days", "gaps between".

**Shape (LEAD method):**
- Dedupe to one row per entity-day.
- `LEAD(day)` per entity -> `next_day`.
- Keep rows where `next_day - day > 1`. Gap = `day + 1` through `next_day - 1`.

**When to use a calendar instead:** the gap can be at the start or end of the period, or the entity has zero rows. Join a calendar table and anti-join.

**No calendar table?** Generate dates with a recursive CTE:
- MySQL: `WITH RECURSIVE cal(d) AS (SELECT DATE '2024-03-01' UNION ALL SELECT d + INTERVAL 1 DAY FROM cal WHERE d < '2024-03-10') ...`
- SQL Server: `WITH cal(d) AS (SELECT CAST('2024-03-01' AS DATE) UNION ALL SELECT DATEADD(day, 1, d) FROM cal WHERE d < '2024-03-10') ... OPTION (MAXRECURSION 400)` (no `RECURSIVE` keyword; default cap is 100 levels).

syntax.mysql:
LEAD(day_col) OVER (PARTITION BY entity ORDER BY day_col)
DATEDIFF(next_day, day_col)
syntax.tsql:
LEAD(day_col) OVER (PARTITION BY entity ORDER BY day_col)
DATEDIFF(day, day_col, next_day)

args.name: next_day
args.meaning: The LEAD result. NULL on each entity's last row, so `NULL > 1` drops it (correct).

args.name: DATEDIFF first arg (T-SQL)
args.meaning: The unit (`day`). MySQL's two-argument form is always days and takes (later, earlier).

examples.title: LEAD to look at the next active day
examples.explain_md: After dedupe, `LEAD` pulls each user's next login date. `gap_days` = 1 means consecutive; the last row per user has no next day (NULL).

tables.name: logins
tables.description_md: One row per login event. User 1 logged in twice on 2024-06-02 (duplicate day). User 4's run crosses a month end.

examples.mysql:
WITH days AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT user_id, login_date FROM logins
)
SELECT user_id, login_date,
       LEAD(login_date) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY login_date) AS next_login,
       DATEDIFF(LEAD(login_date) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY login_date), login_date) AS gap_days
FROM days
ORDER BY user_id, login_date;
examples.tsql:
WITH days AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT user_id, login_date FROM logins
)
SELECT user_id, login_date,
       LEAD(login_date) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY login_date) AS next_login,
       DATEDIFF(day, login_date, LEAD(login_date) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY login_date)) AS gap_days
FROM days
ORDER BY user_id, login_date;
examples.dialect_note_md: Argument order differs: MySQL `DATEDIFF(later, earlier)` returns days; SQL Server `DATEDIFF(day, earlier, later)`.

examples.title: Report each gap as a range of missing days
examples.explain_md: Keep rows where the next day is more than 1 day away. The missing range is `login_date + 1` to `next_login - 1`; the count is `gap_days - 1`. Users 1 and 2 have gaps; users 3 and 4 have none (single day / unbroken).

tables.name: logins
tables.description_md: One row per login event. User 1 logged in twice on 2024-06-02 (duplicate day). User 4's run crosses a month end.

examples.mysql:
WITH days AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT user_id, login_date FROM logins
), nxt AS (
  SELECT user_id, login_date,
         LEAD(login_date) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY login_date) AS next_login
  FROM days
)
SELECT user_id,
       DATE_ADD(login_date, INTERVAL 1 DAY) AS gap_start,
       DATE_SUB(next_login, INTERVAL 1 DAY) AS gap_end,
       DATEDIFF(next_login, login_date) - 1 AS missing_days
FROM nxt
WHERE DATEDIFF(next_login, login_date) > 1
ORDER BY user_id, gap_start;
examples.tsql:
WITH days AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT user_id, login_date FROM logins
), nxt AS (
  SELECT user_id, login_date,
         LEAD(login_date) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY login_date) AS next_login
  FROM days
)
SELECT user_id,
       DATEADD(day, 1, login_date) AS gap_start,
       DATEADD(day, -1, next_login) AS gap_end,
       DATEDIFF(day, login_date, next_login) - 1 AS missing_days
FROM nxt
WHERE DATEDIFF(day, login_date, next_login) > 1
ORDER BY user_id, gap_start;

examples.title: Gaps in a daily series (dataset)
examples.explain_md: West has no row on 03-04 or 03-07, so two one-day gaps. Same recipe, filtered to one region.
examples.mysql:
WITH nxt AS (
  SELECT sale_date,
         LEAD(sale_date) OVER (ORDER BY sale_date) AS next_date
  FROM daily_sales
  WHERE region = 'West'
)
SELECT DATE_ADD(sale_date, INTERVAL 1 DAY) AS gap_start,
       DATE_SUB(next_date, INTERVAL 1 DAY) AS gap_end,
       DATEDIFF(next_date, sale_date) - 1 AS missing_days
FROM nxt
WHERE DATEDIFF(next_date, sale_date) > 1
ORDER BY gap_start;
examples.tsql:
WITH nxt AS (
  SELECT sale_date,
         LEAD(sale_date) OVER (ORDER BY sale_date) AS next_date
  FROM daily_sales
  WHERE region = 'West'
)
SELECT DATEADD(day, 1, sale_date) AS gap_start,
       DATEADD(day, -1, next_date) AS gap_end,
       DATEDIFF(day, sale_date, next_date) - 1 AS missing_days
FROM nxt
WHERE DATEDIFF(day, sale_date, next_date) > 1
ORDER BY gap_start;

examples.title: Calendar anti-join: also catches gaps at the edges
examples.explain_md: `LEAD` cannot see missing days before the first or after the last row. Join a calendar table (one row per date in the period you care about) and keep the dates with no match. If you have no calendar table, generate one with a recursive CTE (see the body above).

tables.name: dim_date
tables.description_md: A calendar table: one row per date, 2024-03-01..03-10.

tables.name: west_sales
tables.description_md: Sales days for the West region only (no sales on 03-04 and 03-07).

examples.mysql:
SELECT c.d AS missing_date
FROM dim_date c
LEFT JOIN west_sales s ON s.sale_date = c.d
WHERE s.sale_date IS NULL
ORDER BY c.d;
examples.tsql:
SELECT c.d AS missing_date
FROM dim_date c
LEFT JOIN west_sales s ON s.sale_date = c.d
WHERE s.sale_date IS NULL
ORDER BY c.d;

pitfalls_md: LEAD only finds gaps between existing rows; leading/trailing gaps need a calendar.
Decide up front whether a gap is 'more than 1 day' or 'more than N days of inactivity'.

sections.heading: Missing ids and id islands
sections.body_md:
**Cue:** "find the missing invoice numbers", "ranges of consecutive ids", "sequence has holes".

**Shape:**
- Missing ranges: `LEAD(id)`, keep `next - id > 1`, report `id+1 .. next-1`.
- Present ranges: `id - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY id)` is the island key.
- First missing id: anti-join the table to itself on `id + 1`.

examples.title: Missing id ranges with LEAD
examples.explain_md: Ids 104, 107-108 and 112-114 are missing. Same LEAD shape on integers: a gap exists where `next_id - invoice_id > 1`.

tables.name: invoices
tables.description_md: Invoice ids that should be gapless from 101 upward. Some were deleted or never issued.

examples.mysql:
WITH nxt AS (
  SELECT invoice_id, LEAD(invoice_id) OVER (ORDER BY invoice_id) AS next_id
  FROM invoices
)
SELECT invoice_id + 1 AS missing_from, next_id - 1 AS missing_to,
       next_id - invoice_id - 1 AS how_many
FROM nxt
WHERE next_id - invoice_id > 1
ORDER BY missing_from;
examples.tsql:
WITH nxt AS (
  SELECT invoice_id, LEAD(invoice_id) OVER (ORDER BY invoice_id) AS next_id
  FROM invoices
)
SELECT invoice_id + 1 AS missing_from, next_id - 1 AS missing_to,
       next_id - invoice_id - 1 AS how_many
FROM nxt
WHERE next_id - invoice_id > 1
ORDER BY missing_from;

examples.title: Islands of consecutive ids: id minus row number
examples.explain_md: No date functions needed: `invoice_id - rn` is constant inside a run. Four runs of ids: 101-103, 105-106, 109-111 and 115 alone.

tables.name: invoices
tables.description_md: Invoice ids that should be gapless from 101 upward. Some were deleted or never issued.

examples.mysql:
WITH numbered AS (
  SELECT invoice_id, invoice_id - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY invoice_id) AS grp
  FROM invoices
)
SELECT MIN(invoice_id) AS first_id, MAX(invoice_id) AS last_id, COUNT(*) AS ids_in_run
FROM numbered
GROUP BY grp
ORDER BY first_id;
examples.tsql:
WITH numbered AS (
  SELECT invoice_id, invoice_id - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY invoice_id) AS grp
  FROM invoices
)
SELECT MIN(invoice_id) AS first_id, MAX(invoice_id) AS last_id, COUNT(*) AS ids_in_run
FROM numbered
GROUP BY grp
ORDER BY first_id;

examples.title: Smallest missing id (self anti-join)
examples.explain_md: An id starts a hole if `id + 1` does not exist. The minimum such `id + 1` is the first missing id. It cannot see a hole before the first id, and `MAX + 1` is always a candidate, which only wins when nothing is missing.

tables.name: invoices
tables.description_md: Invoice ids that should be gapless from 101 upward. Some were deleted or never issued.

examples.mysql:
SELECT MIN(a.invoice_id + 1) AS first_missing
FROM invoices a
LEFT JOIN invoices b ON b.invoice_id = a.invoice_id + 1
WHERE b.invoice_id IS NULL;
examples.tsql:
SELECT MIN(a.invoice_id + 1) AS first_missing
FROM invoices a
LEFT JOIN invoices b ON b.invoice_id = a.invoice_id + 1
WHERE b.invoice_id IS NULL;

pitfalls_md: Holes before the first id or after the last cannot be seen without knowing the expected range (compare to a generated sequence).
Duplicate ids break `id - rn`; dedupe first.

sections.heading: Islands of consecutive status values
sections.body_md:
**Cue:** "how long was the device down in a row", "consecutive rows with the same status", "stretches where the value stayed the same".

**Shape A (two row numbers):** `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY entity ORDER BY ts) - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY entity, status ORDER BY ts)` is constant per run. Group by entity, status, key.

**Shape B (change flag):** `LAG` compare -> 0/1 flag -> running `SUM` = run number. Preferred when the condition is more than simple equality.

examples.title: Two row numbers: overall vs within status
examples.explain_md: `rn_all` counts every reading per machine; `rn_status` counts readings of the same status. While a run continues both rise together so `rn_all - rn_status` is constant; when status flips, one counter stalls and the difference changes.

tables.name: machine_status
tables.description_md: Hourly status readings per machine. Machine 1 flips up/down/up/down; machine 2 stays up.

examples.mysql:
SELECT machine_id, read_ts, status,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY machine_id ORDER BY read_ts) AS rn_all,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY machine_id, status ORDER BY read_ts) AS rn_status,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY machine_id ORDER BY read_ts)
         - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY machine_id, status ORDER BY read_ts) AS grp
FROM machine_status
ORDER BY machine_id, read_ts;
examples.tsql:
SELECT machine_id, read_ts, status,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY machine_id ORDER BY read_ts) AS rn_all,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY machine_id, status ORDER BY read_ts) AS rn_status,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY machine_id ORDER BY read_ts)
         - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY machine_id, status ORDER BY read_ts) AS grp
FROM machine_status
ORDER BY machine_id, read_ts;

examples.title: Collapse each run of the same status
examples.explain_md: `GROUP BY machine_id, status, grp` (status must be in the grouping: two different statuses can share a `grp` value). Machine 1 has 4 runs: up, down, up, down.

tables.name: machine_status
tables.description_md: Hourly status readings per machine. Machine 1 flips up/down/up/down; machine 2 stays up.

examples.mysql:
WITH numbered AS (
  SELECT machine_id, read_ts, status,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY machine_id ORDER BY read_ts)
           - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY machine_id, status ORDER BY read_ts) AS grp
  FROM machine_status
), runs AS (
  SELECT machine_id, status, grp, MIN(read_ts) AS run_start, MAX(read_ts) AS run_end,
         COUNT(*) AS readings
  FROM numbered
  GROUP BY machine_id, status, grp
)
SELECT machine_id, status, run_start, run_end, readings FROM runs ORDER BY machine_id, run_start;
examples.tsql:
WITH numbered AS (
  SELECT machine_id, read_ts, status,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY machine_id ORDER BY read_ts)
           - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY machine_id, status ORDER BY read_ts) AS grp
  FROM machine_status
), runs AS (
  SELECT machine_id, status, grp, MIN(read_ts) AS run_start, MAX(read_ts) AS run_end,
         COUNT(*) AS readings
  FROM numbered
  GROUP BY machine_id, status, grp
)
SELECT machine_id, status, run_start, run_end, readings FROM runs ORDER BY machine_id, run_start;

examples.title: Longest 'down' run per machine
examples.explain_md: Filter the runs to the status you care about, then rank. Machine 2 never went down so it has no row; LEFT JOIN from a machine list if it must show as 0.

tables.name: machine_status
tables.description_md: Hourly status readings per machine. Machine 1 flips up/down/up/down; machine 2 stays up.

examples.mysql:
WITH numbered AS (
  SELECT machine_id, read_ts, status,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY machine_id ORDER BY read_ts)
           - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY machine_id, status ORDER BY read_ts) AS grp
  FROM machine_status
), runs AS (
  SELECT machine_id, status, grp, MIN(read_ts) AS run_start, MAX(read_ts) AS run_end,
         COUNT(*) AS readings
  FROM numbered
  GROUP BY machine_id, status, grp
)
SELECT machine_id, run_start, run_end, readings
FROM (
  SELECT runs.*, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY machine_id ORDER BY readings DESC, run_start) AS rk
  FROM runs
  WHERE status = 'down'
) r
WHERE rk = 1
ORDER BY machine_id;

examples.title: Alternative: flag changes with LAG, then running SUM
examples.explain_md: Mark a row 1 when its status differs from the previous row (first row: `LAG` is NULL, `=` gives NULL, so the ELSE branch gives 1). The running sum is the run number. Same family as sessionization; needs no matched pair of row numbers.

tables.name: machine_status
tables.description_md: Hourly status readings per machine. Machine 1 flips up/down/up/down; machine 2 stays up.

examples.mysql:
WITH flagged AS (
  SELECT machine_id, read_ts, status,
         CASE WHEN status = LAG(status) OVER (PARTITION BY machine_id ORDER BY read_ts)
              THEN 0 ELSE 1 END AS is_new_run
  FROM machine_status
)
SELECT machine_id, read_ts, status, is_new_run,
       SUM(is_new_run) OVER (PARTITION BY machine_id ORDER BY read_ts
                             ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS run_no
FROM flagged
ORDER BY machine_id, read_ts;

pitfalls_md: Group by status as well as the key; different statuses can produce the same key value.
Ties in the ordering column make run boundaries non-deterministic; add a unique tie-breaker.
Use explicit `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` on the running sum; the default `RANGE` frame treats equal timestamps as one step.
